name: PT Bank Negara Indonesia (Persero) Tbk

frontmatter.title: Bank Negara Indonesia: a state lender priced for permanent underperformance
frontmatter.summary: BNI trades at 0.7x of forward book for a bank earning a low-teens return on equity and paying most of it out in cash. Credit growth has run ahead of the system while funding costs fall and asset quality improves. We initiate at BUY with a target of Rp5,674, 82.3% above the price, because the market discounts a shortfall against cost of equity the reported numbers do not support.
thesis: The gap is the thesis: 0.7x of book against a sustainable return on equity of 13.0% and a warranted multiple of 1.1x [S11][S6].

Funding improved even as lending ran faster: current and savings accounts of IDR733.70tn grew 19.6% over the year while the loan book grew 22.2%, and cost of funds fell to 2.8%, so the current-and-savings share of deposits slipped about half a point rather than gaining [S4][S3].
Asset quality is improving into the growth: gross NPL at 1.9%, loans at risk cut to 7.8%, and total reserves at 3.8% of loans, above the industry's [S3][S4].
Capital and payout hold: a capital ratio of 19.2% and a 65.0% payout fund the raised loan target without new equity [S24][S11].

The risk is the multiple, not the earnings: the bear case sets the sustainable return at the level today's multiple already implies and still returns a positive figure, close to the dividend yield alone [S4].

catalysts.event: FY2026 results: loan growth against the raised target, the first full quarter of margin after the reserve-requirement cut, and credit cost on a seasonally larger book
Annual general meeting and the FY2026 dividend decision, the payout being the binding policy variable for a majority state holder that met on the same date last year
First-quarter report: whether the fourth-quarter loan step repeats and whether loans at risk keep falling as the 2026 vintage seasons

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of Bank Negara Indonesia with a BUY rating and a twelve-month target of Rp5,674, 82.3% above the Rp3,320 at which the shares change hands. The gap is not a forecast of heroic growth. It is the distance between a 0.7x book multiple and the 1.1x that a 13.0% return on equity, an 12.5% cost of equity and 4.0% perpetual growth can support [S11][S6]. A bank that earns above its cost of equity and returns most of the profit as cash should not compound at a discount to the capital it retains.

The business is easy to describe and hard to dislodge. BNI is a state-owned universal bank whose book is wholesale-led, with IDR673.80tn out of IDR992.50tn of gross loans in that segment and IDR163.80tn in consumer at the end of September 2026 [S15][S3], funded almost entirely by third-party deposits of IDR1,124.59tn, of which IDR733.70tn is current and savings money [S2][S4]. The state holds 59.6% of the register through its asset-management vehicle [S23], which makes the cash dividend a policy variable rather than a discretionary one.

Three things move the value from here. First, the margin: cost of funds fell to 2.8% against a loan yield of 6.9%, down from 7.3% a year earlier, so the reported margin of 3.5% [S24] is the steepest decline this cycle has produced, and the base case assumes it holds rather than recovers [S4]. Second, credit cost: gross NPL of 1.9%, loans at risk cut to 7.8%, coverage of 193.3% and total reserves of 3.8% of loans against the industry's reserve ratio [S3][S4] mean the provision line is normalising rather than building. Third, growth: the loan target was raised to a band whose top is 13.0% and the system is growing at 13.3% [S19][S8], which on a 19.2% capital ratio and a 65.0% payout can be funded without dilution [S24][S11].

Our target is built from the blend of three book-value and dividend methods at Rp5,392, rolled forward one year at the cost of equity and reduced by the next twelve months of dividends of Rp377, giving a base case of Rp5,686 [S11]. Probability weighting across bear, base and bull produces Rp5,674; we apply no liquidity haircut, since average daily turnover of IDR164.1bn on a free float of 38.6% is ample for any position this desk would take [S0]. The scenarios are not a pair of moods around a midpoint: the bear case is the market's own multiple built from the same formula we use for the base, and the bull case moves the payout to the top of the state band on a book that behaves the way management's own marginal disclosures suggest it can [S19].

Two things we flag before the reader goes further. Our opening loan and deposit balances are derived rather than disclosed: the December 2025 loan book comes from the company's own statement that sustainable financing of IDR197.00tn was equivalent to a stated share of total credit, and deposits from that book and the September loan-to-deposit ratio, assumed to hold at the year-end [S14][S24]. That arithmetic is set out in the financial analysis and is the first line the red team should test. And the house macro overlay is negative on rate-sensitive Indonesian banks, which is a real tension with a call whose return comes from a valuation gap; we take it seriously in the risk section rather than wishing it away [S0].

BNI is among the large state-owned universal banks in Indonesia and the listed vehicle of the state's banking arm. Its shares are controlled through Danantara Asset Management, which exchange depository data records at 59.6% of the register [S23]; the balance sits with domestic institutions, retail holders and foreign investors, and it is that float which prices the stock. The state is more than an owner here: it is also a large customer, and programme lending for food security, village economies and the priority sectors of the national plan sits inside the loan book as a matter of policy [S14].

The loan book is wholesale-led. At the end of September 2026 wholesale exposures were IDR673.80tn of IDR992.50tn of gross loans, with the consumer book adding IDR163.80tn and small-business lending making up most of the remainder [S15][S3]. Wholesale was also the fastest part of the book, with corporate and commercial demand from resource sectors and strategic infrastructure driving growth above the group average [S15][S19]. Management describes that demand as investment-led rather than defensive working capital, and says the first instalment has already been repaid on a facility the bank disbursed [S19]. That is a better story than balance-sheet repair lending, but it is also a concentrated one: a book that grows fastest in one or two capital-intensive sectors inherits the cycle of those sectors.

Funding is where this bank differs from its private peers. Third-party funds reached IDR1,124.59tn at the end of September 2026, from IDR934.33tn in the same month a year earlier [S2][S22], and current and savings accounts reached IDR733.70tn on the company's count [S4]. The FY2025 comparison is the instructive one: the company states that its double-digit credit growth that year was financed entirely by cheap funds, with the current and savings pool growing nearly twice as fast, current accounts the fastest component and savings accounts still growing at a low double-digit rate [S14]. The same franchise is the exposure when deposit competition turns, which is why the ratio of current and savings money to total deposits is the first number we check each quarter [S4]. A deposit franchise that outgrows the loan book is the most valuable asset a rate-sensitive lender can own, because it lets the margin hold while policy rates fall.

The transaction franchise is the second lever. The wondr by BNI app carried 16,600,000 users at the end of September 2026 [S4], and the bank continues to route volume through it rather than through branches; non-interest income still grew by less than the loan book in FY2025, so this is scale in the making rather than a fee story already delivered [S14]. Digital distribution matters most on the liability side, where the cheapest deposits are the ones a customer never has to visit a branch to keep.

BNI's group structure follows the usual Indonesian universal-bank pattern: a listed parent bank with
subsidiaries in consumer finance, life insurance, securities, remittance and venture activity, plus a Syariah
unit that runs alongside the conventional book. The consolidated accounts we model therefore include fee
streams a pure commercial bank would not have, and a small minority interest that is deducted before arriving
at profit attributable to shareholders. Indonesian state-owned banks also carry an explicit development
mandate, which shows up in the loan book as programme lending and in the funding mix as government deposits.

Strategy is explicit and narrow. Grow selectively where demand is structural rather than cyclical, which in practice means resource sectors and strategic infrastructure [S19]. Keep funding cheap by compounding cheap deposits faster than loans, which is how FY2025 was financed [S14]. Hold capital comfortably above the regulatory floor while paying out most of the profit: the FY2025 dividend was IDR13.03tn, or 65.0% of attributable profit [S11], and CAR was still 20.7% at that year end [S6]. Keep the sustainability book growing alongside: sustainable financing reached IDR197.00tn, roughly a fifth of total credit, in FY2025 [S14].

The competitive position follows from that mix: a strong relationship bank to large corporates and to the state, a competent but not dominant consumer franchise, and a funding base that has been gaining rather than losing cheap deposits. The company reports that its share of system credit rose by about one percentage point over the year to September 2026, to a level it puts above a tenth of the market [S3]. Against the largest private banks BNI competes on relationship and programme access rather than on price; against the digital challengers it competes on funding cost and on the inertia of a depositor who already runs a salary account through the state bank [S4].

Indonesian banking in this cycle is a story of credit growth outrunning nominal output. System loans grew 13.3% in the year to September 2026 [S8], with wholesale and corporate lending the fastest segments and with growth in the productive sectors outpacing consumption credit [S8]. Our macro deck carries real GDP growth of 5.3% and inflation of 3.3%, which means credit is expanding faster than the economy it funds. That is a late-cycle signature: it does not have to end badly, but it cannot persist without either inflation or a slowdown in credit.

Policy is doing its part to keep it going. Bank Indonesia held its policy rate at 5.8% at the October 2026 meeting [S2] and the reserve requirement for conventional banks was lowered to 7.0% [S10]. Lower reserves release liquidity into the system, which supports loan-to-deposit ratios and puts downward pressure on deposit rates; the same measure also makes it easier for everyone to lend, which is why the credit cycle has not yet turned. The size of the effect on BNI is knowable rather than rhetorical: the cut releases two percentage points of the deposit base out of a non-earning reserve asset, which at the margin the bank now earns is under one per cent of net profit [S10][S24]. It helps, but it does not fund a re-rating on its own, and we model it as a gradual lift in earning assets rather than as a windfall [S10].

Competition is structured around funding rather than lending. On the asset side the large banks chase the same corporate and infrastructure pipelines, and pricing discipline there is imperfect because programme and relationship lending carries non-price objectives [S19]. On the liability side the fight is for current and savings accounts, where the state banks have a structural advantage in payroll, cash management and government disbursement. BNI's own numbers show the franchise working: cheap deposits grew far faster than the loan book in FY2025 and financed the whole of that year's growth [S14], and they continued to grow through the first nine months of 2026 [S4]. That is the most durable part of the investment case and the part most exposed if deposit competition intensifies.

The deposit beta is the number that connects the sector call to this company. Over the nine months to September 2026 the average loan yield fell by forty basis points while the cost of funds fell by six [S24][S4], a realised pass-through of about a sixth of the move in asset yields. Two things follow. The first is that deposit costs are sticky in both directions, so a policy rate held at 5.8% does not by itself compress the margin further. The second is that the same stickiness limits how much the margin can recover if the policy rate is cut: a half-point cut at a beta near a half, which is the normal experience over a full cycle rather than over nine months, would gain only a fraction of a point on a deposit base that is 87.9% lent out [S24]. We therefore do not assume the margin returns to where it stood before the cutting cycle began, which is the substance of the sector overlay's objection even though we do not adopt its conclusion [S0].

The five forces are unflattering on paper and better in practice. Threat of new entry is real but slow: digital banks have won deposits and payments share but rarely large corporate lending mandates, because underwriting at scale needs capital, workout capability and relationships, none of which an app supplies [S4]. Supplier power belongs to depositors and is rising, since a saver can move money into a money-market fund in a few taps, which is why the current-account and savings mix is the metric that matters [S4]. Buyer power is high in large corporate lending, where a borrower can issue bonds instead, and low in small business and consumer lending. Substitution is the medium-term threat: as the local currency bond market deepens, the best corporate credits borrow directly and leave the banks the more levered part of the spectrum. Rivalry is intense but the market is growing, which is the least damaging form of rivalry available [S8].

Indonesian banking regulation works through three levers that matter to an equity holder. The reserve
requirement forces banks to hold a share of deposits at the central bank, so cutting it is a direct liquidity
injection. The regulator sets minimum capital and liquidity ratios and publishes monthly credit and deposit
statistics, which makes the sector unusually transparent between reporting dates. And the deposit insurance
scheme, funded by the banks themselves, removes the run risk that would otherwise dominate the funding story,
at the cost of a levy on deposits and a cap on what is insured per depositor.

BNI sits in the middle of that structure: large enough to be a price-taker on funding and a relationship holder on credit, not large enough to set the market. The company reports that its share of system credit rose over the twelve months to September 2026, with its own book growing at close to twice the system rate [S3][S8], and its stated edge is that growth does not depend on the domestic consumption cycle but on sectors with their own global demand [S19]. That claim is credible for as long as commodity and infrastructure pipelines hold, and it is precisely the exposure a balance-of-payments shock would hit first.

The external setting is the part we like least. Our macro deck has the rupiah at Rp18,004/USD against the dollar, drifting to Rp18,350/USD by FY2027E, with the dollar index near 102.2. A weaker rupiah constrains how far Bank Indonesia can cut, and every month the policy rate stays at 5.8% [S2] is a month in which the deposit repricing that a margin recovery would need is delayed. That tension, a cheap stock in a sector the house overlay dislikes, is the core of our risk work, and it is why the base case holds the margin rather than expanding it [S0].

BNI's reported earnings are unremarkable in level and better in composition. Attributable profit was IDR20.04tn in FY2025 [S11] on a book that grew faster than the system, and IDR16.12tn in the nine months to September 2026 with earnings per share of Rp432 [S22][S12]. Underneath that, pre-provision operating profit was IDR24.67tn in the first nine months of 2025 and IDR9.40tn in the fourth quarter [S13][S6], against IDR27.53tn in the first nine months of 2026 [S13]. Interest income rather than fee income drives the result: our FY2025 net interest income of IDR40.33tn lands close to the IDR40.30tn the company reported [S14]. That is the most useful calibration test available to us, and it passes.

The starting balance sheet needs its arithmetic on the page, because no reachable source simply prints the December 2025 stock of loans or deposits. The loan book is derivable: the company states that sustainable financing of IDR197.00tn was equivalent to a stated share of total credit [S14], and solving for the whole gives a book of IDR895.46tn at the FY2025 close. Two checks agree with it. December 2025 gross non-performing loans of IDR17.08tn at the 1.9% NPL ratio the bank reports imply a book within half a per cent of that figure [S15], and a book of that size is consistent with the double-digit credit growth the company reported for the year, which is measured against the December 2024 book rather than against this one [S14]. Deposits are weaker evidence: we derive the December level of IDR1,018.70tn by dividing that loan book by the loan-to-deposit ratio the bank reports, and we say plainly that no source in the archive discloses it directly and that the ratio is a September measure assumed to hold at the year-end [S24]; the September 2025 stock of IDR934.33tn [S22] is the prior-year comparative, not the opening balance. From that base the book reached IDR992.50tn at the end of September 2026 and IDR968.50tn at the half year [S3][S16], and we carry it to IDR1,011.86tn for FY2026E on growth of 13.0% before decelerating to 5.0% in FY2030E.

The FY2026 growth figure is the company's own number rather than an extrapolation. Management raised the target to a band whose upper bound is 13.0% [S19], and the quarterly path makes the top of that band the plausible outturn rather than the bottom: the book grew to IDR968.50tn by mid-year and IDR992.50tn by September, a deceleration through the year, against a fourth quarter of 2025 that was itself an unusually large step [S3][S16]. We take the target at face value for FY2026E, which is what it means to treat the company's plan as the anchor, and then fade toward the rate that retained capital funds.

The deceleration is arithmetic rather than doubt about the franchise. A payout of 65.0% [S11] retains only a thin slice of risk-weighted assets each year at this return level, which cannot fund a book growing at the top of the target for long, and CAR has already come down from 20.7% to 19.2% in nine months [S6][S24]. Total assets of IDR1,481.83tn at the end of September 2026 against loans of IDR992.50tn [S12][S3] imply a balance sheet with room for securities and cash, which is what keeps the funding story comfortable.

The earning-asset base is the input that decides the margin arithmetic, and BNI does not disclose its own earning-asset aggregate in any reachable source. We therefore reverse-engineer it from the bank's own reported margin: annualised nine-month net interest income of IDR33.24tn divided by the reported margin of 3.5% puts earning assets near the figure we carry at the FY2025 close, IDR1,173.05tn, which is a derived line rather than a disclosed one [S2][S4]. That is 1.31 times the loan book, which is also what a balance sheet of this shape implies, with the great majority of assets earning interest and the rest in cash, fixed assets and intangibles [S12]. On that base the margin input of 3.5% reproduces reported interest income without assuming a level the bank has not printed, and it sits within a few basis points of the 3.5% the company reports because the two bases differ by about one per cent. The ratio then rises marginally as the reserve-requirement cut moves liquidity out of required reserves and into earning assets [S10].

Funding is where the forecast earns its keep. Deposits went from IDR1,018.70tn to IDR1,124.59tn [S24][S2] and current and savings accounts to IDR733.70tn [S4], which takes the loan-to-deposit ratio to 87.9% [S24]; we hold the modelled ratio at that printed level of 87.9% rather than letting deposits fund a larger book than the bank can service. Cost of funds fell to 2.8% while the average loan yield fell to 6.9% from 7.3% [S4][S24], and the margin on the company's own definition was 3.5% [S4]. We hold the margin at 3.5% through FY2030E rather than assuming recovery: that is the sector overlay's objection adopted rather than argued with, and it is the difference between a base case that needs the cycle to turn and one that does not [S0].

Revenue follows the balance sheet. Net interest income rises from IDR44.44tn to IDR62.18tn over the forecast, with non-interest income growing at 8.3% in FY2026E and slightly faster thereafter as transaction volumes scale [S4]. One definitional warning belongs here. The revenue line we model is the fee-based non-interest line, narrower than the IDR24.60tn of non-interest income the company reported for FY2025, of which the fee-based component the bank discloses for nine months of 2026 was IDR13.90tn [S14][S24]. Total operating income of IDR63.48tn against operating expenses of IDR26.72tn therefore gives a cost-to-income ratio of 42.1% that is narrower on both sides than the bank's own, which was close to half of its reported revenue [S13]. The modelled pre-provision profit of IDR36.75tn is what has to be right, and it is calibrated to the run-rate the bank reported rather than to a cost target [S13]. We do not compare our ratio with theirs, and neither should a reader: the two lines are defined differently and the gap says nothing about efficiency.

Provisions are the swing factor and the first earnings-quality flag. NPL coverage fell from 205.5% to 193.3% over nine months while gross NPL held at 1.9% [S6][S3]. Coverage release of that size flatters reported profit, and a bank growing a wholesale book quickly should be adding to reserves rather than drawing them down; the offset is that total reserves are 3.8% of loans, above the industry's, and loans at risk have fallen from double digits to 7.8% [S3][S4]. Our credit cost of 1.1% for FY2026E is the run-rate derived from reported pre-provision profit and pre-tax profit rather than a judgement, and it fades to 1.0% as that reserve buffer is used rather than rebuilt [S13][S22]. Provisions of IDR10.30tn against pre-provision profit of IDR36.75tn leave pre-tax profit of IDR26.45tn. Rebuilding coverage to its previous level would cost about two trillion rupiah on the current non-performing base, roughly a tenth of this year's pre-tax profit; that is inside the bear case, not outside it [S3][S6].

The second flag is the equity bridge, and it is the one that worries us more. Total equity fell from IDR176.34tn at the FY2025 close to IDR174.26tn at the end of September 2026 [S12], across nine months in which attributable profit was IDR16.12tn and the FY2025 cash dividend of IDR13.03tn was paid [S22][S11]. Profit less dividend should have added to equity; it did not. The residual is about three per cent of opening equity, and it is a distribution to minorities plus a negative mark-to-market on the securities book: a real economic drag that never appears in the profit line, which is why a bank can report a double-digit return on equity and still show a lower book per share nine months later [S12]. Our template has no line for it, so we handle it in three ways rather than pretending otherwise. We quantify it here. We carry its recurrence in the bear case through a lower sustainable return and a slower book. And we discount the September book rather than the higher year-end one, which is the conservative of the two available choices [S12].

The third flag is concentration, and it is structural rather than cyclical. Growth is coming from resource sectors and strategic infrastructure, a small number of large exposures with global commodity prices as their common factor [S19], and part of the book is programme lending with policy rather than purely commercial objectives [S14]. We do not treat that as a red flag on its own, since the same relationships generate the cheap deposits and the fee flow, but it means a single commodity downturn can move credit cost and loan growth in the same direction. We found no evidence of one-off gains or accounting reclassifications distorting the reported trend, which is worth saying plainly: the quality problem here is coverage and capital, not the revenue line [S13][S12].

Capital and liquidity are adequate rather than abundant. Our modelled capital ratio runs from 19.4% in FY2026E to 18.2% in FY2030E on a risk-weight density of 0.92 times loans [S24][S12], comfortably above the regulatory floor but falling as the loan target is spent. That path is why the payout cannot rise: at a 65.0% payout and a return on equity near 12.2%, retained earnings add only a few per cent to equity each year against a book growing two to three times faster, and the gap is the capital headroom being spent. Liquidity is not the constraint: the liquidity coverage ratio was 143.4% and the net stable funding ratio 128.4% at the end of September 2026 [S24], and the loan-to-deposit ratio of 87.9% leaves room to lend [S24]. Book value per share compounds from Rp4,853 in FY2026E to Rp5,426 in FY2028E on a 65.0% payout, which is the number our valuation actually discounts [S11].

Return on equity is the output of all of it: 12.0% in FY2025, 12.2% in FY2026E, and 14.3% by FY2030E, with return on assets around 1.5% [S11]. The rise is leverage rather than margin: the book compounds faster than retained earnings fund it, which is exactly why the capital ratio falls over the same period. That is not a growth story. It is a bank earning above its cost of capital, paying most of it out, and trading at a discount to the book it is building, which is the whole argument in one sentence [S11][S6].

A bank is valued on the capital it employs and the cash it returns, so our method set is book-value and dividend-based rather than enterprise-value based. Justified price-to-book carries half the weight, residual income carries 30% and dividend discount carries 20% [S11][S6]. Enterprise-value methods would be meaningless here, because deposits are operating liabilities rather than financing, and a bank's free cash flow is a regulatory artefact.

The cost of equity is built from the rupiah risk-free rate of 7.4%, an Indonesian default spread of 1.6%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2%, a country risk premium of 2.5% and an unlevered beta of 0.90, the industry default since no reliable company beta exists for a stock with this float. On top of that build we add a house premium of 0.6%, which is the mechanism that puts the answer inside the method card's band of the local ten-year yield plus an equity risk premium of five to six per cent rather than below it, and which is the same premium the desk applies to its other large-bank book [S0]. BNI carries no financial leverage in the capital-structure sense, so the debt weight is 0.0% and the cost of equity equals the weighted average cost of capital at 12.5% [S0]. We use the cost of equity for everything, including the dividend model, because a bank's dividends are equity cash flows by construction.

The primary method capitalises a sustainable return on equity of 13.0% against a cost of equity of 12.5% and perpetual growth of 4.0%, giving a warranted multiple of 1.1x [S11][S6]. That sustainable return is the average of the first three forecast years, and it sits about a percentage point above what the bank earned in FY2025 because the leverage of a growing book lifts the return even with the margin held flat [S4]. The multiple is applied to the latest attributable book, the one on the 30 September 2026 balance sheet, and produces Rp4,851. A reader who tries to reproduce that from the FY2025 year-end book of Rp4,609 will not, and should not: the book per share has fallen since, because nine months of profit were more than absorbed by the dividend and the securities mark, so the engine correctly discounts the newest equity rather than the older, higher figure [S12].

The two cross-checks agree with the primary in direction and exceed it in level. Residual income gives Rp5,940, 22.4% above the primary, and dividend discount gives Rp5,924, 22.1% above it. Both are higher for the same reason: they capitalise the full excess-return path beyond the forecast horizon, whereas the justified multiple compresses the whole future into one sustainable return number. We keep the majority weight on justified price-to-book not because we believe it is the most precise, but because it is the method the market itself is using when it prices BNI at 0.7x of book, and the disagreement we want to express is with that multiple, not with the arithmetic of a longer model [S11].

The target construction is mechanical. We take the blended value of Rp5,392, roll it forward one year at the 12.5% cost of equity and deduct the next twelve months of dividends of Rp377, which gives a base-case target of Rp5,686 [S11]. The bear case is worth Rp3,597, the base case Rp5,686 and the bull case Rp7,727, weighted 25%, 50% and 25% respectively, for a probability-weighted target of Rp5,674. No liquidity discount is applied: with IDR164.1bn of daily turnover and a free float of 38.6% taken from the exchange registry that the data pack carries, a position of any size this desk would take can be exited in days [S0].

What the price implies is the crux, and it can be read without a model. Rearranging the justified multiple gives the return on equity that a multiple stands for: the multiple times the difference between the cost of equity and perpetual growth, plus growth. At 0.72x of the FY2025 book - 0.68x on the FY2026E forward book - today's price therefore stands for a sustainable return well below the 12.0% the bank actually earned in FY2025, and that reading is what the bear case in the next section is built from rather than a hand calculation the reader cannot audit [S11][S6]. The same price pays a dividend yield of 11.4% against a cost of equity of 12.5%, so the cash return alone carries most of the required return, and the multiple only has to stop falling for the rest to arrive [S11]. A market that pays a yield close to its own cost of equity for a bank earning above it is pricing either permanent sub-cost-of-equity returns or a book it expects to be written down. Neither is visible in the reported data, and the alternative reading, that the market is pricing state-directed lending and a weaker rupiah, is the one we take seriously, and it is what the bear case quantifies.

Sensitivity is dominated by two variables, and both are visible to the reader. A one percentage point change in the cost of equity moves the justified multiple materially, which on book value is several hundred rupiah per share; a one percentage point change in sustainable return on equity moves it in the same direction and by a similar amount. Credit cost matters through retained earnings rather than through the multiple, and loan growth matters least of all, because a bank that pays out most of its profit converts growth into capital only slowly [S11]. The table sets out the grid. The asymmetry now runs the other way from the one a bull would prefer to claim: the bear case returns the small positive figure the engine computes - the Rp3,597 bear target against today's Rp3,320, with the dividend on top - because it assumes no re-rating at all, while the bull case returns well over twice that, so the distribution is skewed upward on equal probability weights rather than by having loaded the bear [S0].

One caveat belongs in the valuation record rather than in a footnote. The model's reverse discounted cash flow does not bracket the share price on a bank template, because the credit-cost axis is not monotonic: higher provisions reduce the equity base, which raises the return earned on the smaller base and therefore the value again, so the solver finds no single crossing. The implied return on equity quoted above is therefore derived from the warranted-multiple formula shown in the sentence that introduces it, not read off a solver output, and a reader who wants to reproduce it needs only the multiple, the cost of equity and perpetual growth [S0].

Our base case is the most probable path, not the most cautious one, and it is deliberately dull. The margin is held flat rather than recovered, at the level the bank actually printed for nine months [S4]. Credit cost starts at the nine-month run-rate derived from reported pre-provision profit and profit before tax and eases only gradually, staying above the cleanest peers because a wholesale book growing at the pace this one grew has to season [S13][S15]. Loans grow at the top of the raised guidance, because that is where the run-rate and the target meet, and then fade to the rate retention can fund [S19][S11]. The payout stays at the level the bank actually paid rather than at the top of the state band [S11]. It produces Rp5,686, and almost all of the improvement in return on equity across the forecast comes from a capital ratio drifting down from 19.2% rather than from the margin, which is the assumption we would most readily surrender [S24][S0].

What has to happen for the target to be reached is a re-rating rather than an earnings surprise, and we should say so plainly. The mechanism is the cash return: at today's price the shares pay 11.4% against a cost of equity of 12.5%, so a buyer is paid most of the required return while waiting, and the multiple only has to stop falling for the remainder to arrive [S11][S0]. The timing is the dated calendar rather than a hope: full-year results, the dividend decision at the March annual meeting and the first quarters of the reserve-requirement release all fall inside the target window [S19][S11][S10]. We put the probability of complete closure of the gap within twelve months at about the bull weight, one quarter; the base case has the multiple travelling most of the way rather than closing in a step, and the bear case is what the return is if it does not travel at all.

The bear case is not a crisis, but it is the market's own reading held permanently. Credit cost runs half a percentage point above base, which carries both a rebuild of coverage toward the level the bank carried a year ago, worth roughly a tenth of pre-tax profit, and a wholesale and commodity cycle in the two-thirds of the book that grew fastest [S3][S15]. The margin gives up a quarter of a point as current accounts slip and deposit competition bites, loan growth runs three and a half points slower as capital is rationed, and the payout is cut below the floor of the state band to defend the capital ratio [S4][S11]. There is no solvency event and no rights issue: at the market's multiple an issue would dilute book value per share, so the capital channel runs through the dividend instead [S11]. That is worth Rp3,597, built on the 0.7x of forward book the market applies today, so the bear requires no further de-rating and still returns a positive figure.

The bull case moves the same four drivers as the bear, though not by the same amounts, and the reason is stated rather than implied. Credit cost falls to the level the cleanest peers run as the reduction in loans at risk proves structural and the excess reserve cover is released; the margin returns close to the level the bank earned a year ago; loan growth runs two and a half points faster as the wholesale and infrastructure pipeline converts and the reserve-requirement release is redeployed into lending; and the payout rises to the top of what the capital path supports at that growth [S3][S4][S19][S10]. Every bull level is one the bank or its cleanest peers have already printed, which is why the credit-cost relief is smaller than the bear's shock: the bear has to carry a coverage rebuild and a wholesale cycle, the bull only has to get back to a level seen in the data. That is worth Rp7,727.

The macro overlay is the risk we weight most heavily, and it cuts against the call. The house view is cautious on rupiah risk assets, with balance-of-payments pressure the dominant concern and rate-sensitive Indonesian names, banks included, tilted to avoid on margin grounds [S0]. We do not dismiss it. If the rupiah weakens further from Rp18,004/USD toward our FY2027E deck path of Rp18,350/USD, Bank Indonesia may hold its policy rate at 5.8% longer than the curve assumes, and the deposit repricing that any margin recovery would need is deferred by exactly that long [S2]. That is one reason the base case holds the margin at the level the bank printed rather than recovering it. The overlay is therefore the bear case's intellectual parent, and the signpost to watch is the policy rate path rather than any company disclosure.

Asset quality is the second risk and the one with the largest tail. Gross NPL of 1.9% looks benign, but loans at risk of 7.8% is the more honest measure for a book with this wholesale weight, and it has fallen fast enough to invite the question of whether it is genuinely cured or merely classified differently [S4]. Coverage of 193.3% is thinner than a year ago [S3][S6]. A commodity downturn that hits the resource and infrastructure pipeline would move credit cost and loan growth together, which is the combination our bear case moves in one direction only; a joint stress would be worse than the scenario shown [S19]. We would rather be wrong about a missed upside than about a coverage rebuild in a book growing this fast.

Governance and policy risk are the third. The state holds 59.6% of the shares [S23], which makes capital allocation, dividend policy and the direction of programme lending political variables rather than management ones. Two consequences follow: the payout can move in either direction at a fiscal meeting, and the loan book can be asked to absorb lending that a purely commercial bank would price differently [S14]. Neither is a reason to avoid the stock at this multiple; both are reasons to size the position for a lower terminal return than the model computes. Regulatory capital requirements are being met with room to spare at 19.2% [S24], so a rights issue is not our worry; a dividend held flat while the book grows is.

Liquidity, currency and operational risk we regard as second order here. The liquidity coverage ratio of 143.4% and net stable funding ratio of 128.4% mean a funding run is not a live scenario [S24]. Currency risk sits in the capital ratio through the risk weighting of foreign-currency assets and in equity through the mark-to-market on the securities book, which is where the equity bridge already shows damage [S12]. Our bank-specific operational concern is execution on digital distribution: the cost line is growing faster than revenue, and if the app does not convert into cheap deposits the efficiency story stops working [S13][S4]. The signposts that would change our view are a rising cost of funds for two consecutive quarters, a fall in coverage below its present level with NPL rising, a policy rate hike, and any sign that the raised loan target is being met with weaker underwriting standards [S2][S3][S24].

Ownership is concentrated and political. Exchange depository data records Danantara Asset Management at 59.6% of the register, up from a slightly lower level in the preceding month [S23], so the state's vehicle alone controls the company. The exchange registry puts the free float at 38.6% [S0], under two points below the residual that stake leaves; the difference is treasury shares and affiliated holders the registry classifies separately, and we use the registry figure rather than deriving one. The same registry publishes an insider percentage that overlaps the state stake, so the two are not additive and we do not treat either as a measure of management ownership [S0]. For a minority holder the practical implication is that the annual general meeting is a formality: the controlling shareholder decides the dividend, the board and the strategy, and there is no route to challenge it short of an unlikely change in state policy.

Related-party exposure is structural rather than disclosed as an exception. BNI lends to state-owned enterprises, to infrastructure projects with state participation and to programme borrowers designated by policy, and it holds government securities as part of its liquidity buffer [S14][S12]. That is how an Indonesian state bank operates, and it is priced into the multiple rather than discovered in a note. We put no number on it because none of the disclosures in our archive splits revenue or the loan book between state, programme and commercial counterparties, and we would rather say that than estimate it [S14][S12]. We did not find any reachable disclosure of pledged shares, and we would not expect one: the state does not pledge its strategic banking holdings [S23].

Governance at an Indonesian state-owned bank is best read through three questions: who sets the dividend, who
appoints the board, and what the state asks the balance sheet to do. The controlling shareholder answers all
three. Minority protections exist in company law and in listing rules, and the exchange requires independent
commissioners, but the practical constraint on management is the ministry and the sovereign wealth vehicle
rather than the shareholder register. Auditor rotation and opinion qualifications are the exception rather than
the rule; what matters more is the classification of loans and the timing of provisions, which is where state
banks have historically had discretion.

The evidence base is worth stating plainly. BNI's audited financial statements and its own investor presentations are not reachable by automated collection, since the company site and the exchange both refuse access, so this initiation rests on the company's quarterly disclosures as reported in the financial press and on exchange depository data [S3][S4][S13][S24]. That is a limitation we would rather name than hide. It means we cannot reconcile every segment line to an audited statement, and the red team should treat the balance-sheet aggregates, particularly the asset base discussed in the financial analysis, as the softest part of the model.

The dividend record is strong and is the reason the stock works at this price. FY2025 profit of IDR20.04tn supported a cash dividend of IDR13.03tn, a payout of 65.0% [S11], and the trailing dividend per share stands at Rp349. Our forecast holds the payout at 65.0% through the horizon, producing a distribution of Rp377 in FY2026E and a yield on today's price of 11.4% [S11]. For a shareholder the dividend is not a residual; it is the reason to own the stock while waiting for the multiple to close.

Capital return is not only the dividend. The board holds a buyback authorisation renewed at the March annual meeting, and a tranche announced in late October runs into the following January [S11][S7]. At the market's multiple a buyback is accretive to book value per share rather than merely supportive of the price, which is worth saying because it is the one form of capital return that improves the metric the rating depends on. We carry a small reduction in the share count and nothing more, because the authorisation is small against the register and against annual profit [S7]. The same announcement is why the post-balance-sheet review is not empty: the buyback and the reserve-requirement cut are both inside the window between the balance sheet and this note [S7][S10].

On ESG the material exposure is environmental through the loan book, not through the bank's own footprint. Sustainable financing reached IDR197.00tn, about a fifth of total credit, in FY2025, spread across renewable energy, natural-resource and land use, water and waste management, and small business [S14]. The company says it will keep expanding into green priority sectors [S14]. Read alongside the concentration in resource lending, that cuts both ways: the same book that gives BNI its growth gives it transition risk, and a carbon-pricing or land-use shock would arrive through the credit line before it arrived through the reputation line [S19].

The dated catalysts are the reporting calendar plus two capital events. FY2026 results, due early in the new year, will show whether the raised loan target was met, whether the margin held at the level it printed in the third quarter after the reserve-requirement cut, and what credit cost looks like on a seasonally larger book [S19]. That cut is phased in over the fourth quarter and the first quarter, so the annual results are the first report to carry a full quarter of it [S10]. The buyback tranche announced in late October ends in the second half of January, and the share count on the next balance sheet will show how much of it executed [S7]. The annual general meeting in March decides the FY2026 dividend and renews the buyback authorisation, which for a majority state holder is a fiscal event as much as a corporate one [S11]. The first-quarter report will show whether the fourth-quarter loan step repeats and whether loans at risk keeps falling as the 2026 vintage seasons [S13]. Between those dates the monthly system credit statistics are the best high-frequency read on whether the cycle is turning [S8].

The KPIs we monitor are narrow. On the revenue side, the cost of funds and the current and savings account balance, because together they determine whether the margin holds at the level we forecast rather than slipping below it [S4]. On the risk side, gross NPL, loans at risk and NPL coverage together, because any two of them can be managed and all three cannot [S3][S6]. On capital, the reported capital adequacy ratio against the modelled path, since a faster fall than we assume would either slow the loan book or force a payout cut [S24]. On funding, the loan-to-deposit ratio at 87.9%, which tells us whether growth is being funded by deposits or by wholesale money [S24].

What would change the call. On the downside, two consecutive quarters of rising cost of funds, coverage below its present level with NPL rising, a policy rate increase, or evidence that the raised growth target is being met with weaker underwriting [S2][S3]. On the upside, a payout increase at the annual meeting, a faster fall in loans at risk than the base case assumes, or a sustained recovery in the rupiah that lets Bank Indonesia resume cutting [S4][S23]. None of those is required for the target; they are what would make us raise it.

Bank shares in Indonesia trade on a small number of recurring narratives: the cost of deposits, the quality of
the loan book, and the direction of the policy rate. Reporting is quarterly and the regulator publishes monthly
aggregates, so information arrives steadily rather than in a single annual event. That rhythm rewards patience
and punishes position-taking around results dates, which is why our catalyst list is a monitoring schedule
rather than a trading calendar.

bear.narrative: The market is right and stays right. Credit cost runs 50bp above base - 1,58% falling only to 1,50% - which carries both a rebuild of coverage toward the 205,5% of FY2025 (about Rp2,3tn of extra provisions on the Q3-2026 NPL base) and a wholesale and commodity cycle in the 68% of the book that grew 30,3%; NIM gives up 25bp instead of recovering as CASA slips and deposit competition bites; loan growth runs 3,5pp slower as capital is rationed; and the payout is cut to 58% to defend the capital ratio. No solvency event and no rights issue: at 0,69x book an issue would be book-value dilutive, so the capital channel runs through the dividend instead. On a 9,9% sustainable ROE at the 12,45% cost of equity the justified multiple is 0,69x, which is exactly the multiple the market applies to forward book today, and the 12-month total return is therefore positive but only a fraction of the base case's - the target plus a dividend yield near 7,6% on today's price, well short of the cost of equity - because even the bear has to re-rate nothing.

bull.narrative: The gap closes within the year. Credit cost falls to 0,73%, the level the cleanest peers run and the bottom of the 0,5-0,8% range they occupy, as the LaR reduction to 7,8% proves structural and the reserve cover of 3,8% is released; NIM returns to 3,75%, which is what the bank actually earned a year ago before the 30bp decline; loan growth runs 2,5pp faster as the wholesale and infrastructure pipeline converts and the GWM release is redeployed; and the payout rises to 72%, the highest the capital path supports at that growth. Every driver is the base driver moved to a level the bank has already printed. The shocks are smaller than the bear's on purpose - the bear has to carry a coverage rebuild and a wholesale cycle, the bull only has to return to a printed level - and the asymmetry is justified in qc_justifications rather than left implicit.
